Annotations 73 LITTLE BUNNY 5 “Every marriage has a score. Most couples just never look at it.” — Little Bunny LITTLE BUNNY 7 — I — The Chairs Every marriage has two chairs. You know this already. What you may not have considered is that the distance between those chairs, and the angle at which they face each other, changes the nature of every conversation that happens between them. The PLT Framework does not claim that marriage

is a transaction or that love is a performance. It claims something more precise: that the language two people use with each other, over time and under pressure, either builds alignment or erodes it. And that alignment can be scored — not to judge, not to keep tally, but to see clearly what is actually happening versus what both people believe is happening. This book documents scored conversations from real marriages. Some of the people whose conversations appear here know the Framework. Most did not, at the time these conversations occurred. The scores were applied retroactively. In every case, the people involved recognized themselves in the annotations. That recognition — I have been told, more than once — was the most useful thing they got from the book. Not the scores themselves. The fact that there was a structure operating beneath what they thought was just chaos. The marriage was always having a conversation about the conversation. This book makes that second conversation visible. LITTLE BUNNY 25 — III — First Year · Scored The first year of a marriage produces a particular class of conversation: high stakes, low information. The two people are still building their shared language. They have not yet learned each other’s tells, defaults, or thresholds. This makes first-year exchanges simultaneously the most volatile and the

most revealing. The patterns that form here tend to calcify. PARTNER A 5 "I feel like you’re not really listening when I talk about my work. You get this look." PLT NOTE: Score 5: Valid observation, but ‘I feel like’ is hedging. She has specific data (the look) but packages it in impressionistic language. The message arrives softened to the point where he can dismiss it without engaging the substance. PARTNER B 6 "I’m listening. I just don’t always know what you need from me when you tell me about it." PLT NOTE: Score 6: Honest and structurally interesting — he’s identifying a real gap. But he led with a defense before acknowledging what she said. The defense lands first. This is a sequencing error the Framework flags in early-marriage conversations. PARTNER A 8 "I don’t always need you to fix it. Sometimes I just need you to stay with me in it." PLT NOTE: Score 8: This is high-precision language under emotional pressure. She defined what she needed without attacking his pattern. ‘Stay with me in it’ is language that could change the next ten years of their conversations if he hears it. PARTNER B 7 "I didn’t know that. I’ll try to do that." PLT NOTE: Score 7: Clean receipt. No defense, no qualification. The score would be

higher if he reflected the language back (‘stay with you in it’) to confirm understanding, but the willingness to receive without defending is already above average for year one. LITTLE BUNNY 35 — IV — The Arguments That Are Not Arguments The Framework distinguishes between two types of conflict in a marriage: alignment conflicts and language conflicts. An alignment conflict is a real disagreement — two people want different things. A language conflict is a disagreement about what was said, meant, or heard. Most couples believe they are having alignment conflicts. Most of what they are actually having are language conflicts. This distinction matters because the resolution strategies are different. An alignment conflict requires negotiation. A language conflict requires translation. Applying a negotiation strategy to a language conflict produces resentment on both sides, because neither person feels heard. The problem was never the position. The problem was the gap between what was said and what arrived. PARTNER B 4 "You always make plans without asking me first. It’s like my schedule doesn’t matter." PLT NOTE: Score 4: ‘Always’ is a red flag in the Framework. It forecloses the conversation before it starts by making a categorical claim that the other person will immediately begin disproving rather than hearing. PARTNER A 3 "That’s not true. I asked you about last weekend."

PLT NOTE: Score 3: He took the ‘always’ bait. Now the conversation is about the word ‘always’, not about the pattern she’s describing. Both people will lose this exchange because they are no longer talking about the same thing. PARTNER B 5 "That was one time. I’m talking about the pattern." PLT NOTE: Score 5: She’s correct that she was talking about the pattern. But she had the tool available — ‘I’m talking about the pattern’ — and didn’t deploy it at the start. It arrives late, after damage. PLT Framework · Language vs. Alignment Conflict After the annotations were shared with the couple in this exchange, Partner B said: ‘I didn’t know I was doing the “always” thing. I do it every time I’m scared he won’t take me seriously.’ This is the diagnostic value of scored conversations. The score reveals not just what was said but what the language was protecting. LITTLE BUNNY 55 — VI — The Repair Conversation The repair conversation is the most technically demanding exchange in a marriage. It arrives after damage — after an argument that ended badly, after a silence that lasted too long, after something that was said that both people know cannot be unsaid. The repair conversation requires the practitioner to be simultaneously honest about what happened, accountable for their

part, and future-oriented about what changes. Most people attempt only one or two of these three components. Pure honesty without accountability produces an autopsy. Pure accountability without honesty produces a performance. Future orientation without honesty or accountability produces a contract that neither person believes in. The Framework holds that all three must be present for the repair to actually close the distance. PARTNER A 9 "I’ve been thinking about what I said. I was wrong to say it that way. I was frustrated and I aimed it at you and that wasn’t fair." PLT NOTE: Score 9: This is a textbook repair opener. Three moves in sequence: acknowledgment, ownership, context. He did not lead with the context (which would be an excuse) — he led with the ownership and placed the context after. Sequencing is everything in repair language. PARTNER B 8 "Thank you for saying that. I need you to know that I heard it as something bigger than you probably meant it to be." PLT NOTE: Score 8: She received the repair cleanly and then offered her own disclosure — her experience of the damage. This is the correct reciprocal move. The repair conversation requires both parties to be vulnerable in sequence, not simultaneously. PARTNER A 9 "Tell me what you heard." PLT NOTE: Score 9: Three words.

He asked her to describe her experience rather than guessing or defending. This is the highest-level move available in a repair conversation — it places the work in the right hands at the right time. LITTLE BUNNY 73 — VIII — Annotations The marriages documented in this volume span four years to thirty-one years of partnership. The Framework scores identically across that range because the structural dynamics of language under intimacy do not change with tenure. If anything, they become more entrenched. Long-term couples have the most established patterns, which makes those patterns both the hardest to see and the most consequential to address. The highest-scoring exchanges in this volume all share a common feature: both partners are precise without being rigid. They say what they mean. They leave room for the other person to revise. They are not performing. Precision without rigidity is the technical definition of mature language in the Framework. It is also what most people describe as love, when they are trying to say something true about it. The score is not the marriage. The score is the map. — Little Bunny
